# How credential resolution works

This document explains *why* the CLI finds your token the way it does — the
precedence order, the "nearest wins" walk-up, and how absence is told apart from
a broken file. It's background reading; for the mechanical rules see the
[Credential Discovery reference](../reference/credential-discovery.md).

## Why env-first, then a walk-up, then home

When a command needs a token, the CLI checks the `GLASSFROG_TOKEN` environment
variable first, then a `.glassfrogrc` walking up from the current directory to
the filesystem root (nearest file wins), then the home-directory file. The first
source that yields a usable token wins.

Two alternatives were considered and rejected:

- **Check only the current directory, then home (no ascent).** This was rejected
  because the design deliberately borrows npm's walk-up model, so a token stored
  near the top of a project applies across the whole subtree — you don't have to
  store it in every working directory.
- **Merge values across all files (npm-style layered config).** Rejected because
  a single token has nothing to merge; "nearest wins" *is* the entire semantic. A
  layered merge would add machinery with no consumer.

The environment variable comes first because the CLI's usual operator is an AI
agent that may inject a token at runtime without writing anything to disk. An
empty or whitespace-only value is ignored rather than treated as a token, so a
blank `GLASSFROG_TOKEN` (common in CI) doesn't shadow a real file — it falls
through to the file search.

A subtlety the design handles explicitly: the home directory can itself be an
ancestor of where you're standing. The candidate list is built ordered and
de-duplicated — start directory, each ancestor up to the root, then home if it
wasn't already visited — so a home file on the ascent path is read exactly once,
at its natural position.

## Why a tokenless file doesn't stop the search

A `.glassfrogrc` that exists and parses but has no usable `token` entry is
*skipped*, and the search continues. The reasoning: a present-but-tokenless
nearest file should not shadow a home file that does have a token, or you'd get a
spurious "no credentials" when a perfectly good credential sits one level up.

## Why absence and breakage are different outcomes

Discovery returns a `Resolution` carrying the token, its `Source`
(`Environment` / `File` / `None`), and the file `Path`. Crucially, `Source: None`
— "nothing found anywhere" — is a **normal** outcome, not an error. A read or
parse failure of a file that *does* exist is a typed error naming the path.

The alternatives, both rejected:

- **A sentinel `ErrNoCredentials` for absence.** Rejected because absence is an
  expected, routine outcome the consumer handles all the time; modelling it as an
  error blurs it with genuine I/O and format failures and complicates branching.
- **Returning only the bare token string.** Rejected because it loses the source
  (needed for the "acting as" line a consumer shows the operator) and can't
  distinguish absence from a broken file.

This three-way split — found / none / error — is what lets [Request
Authentication](why-refuse-rather-than-send-anonymous.md) give you the right next
step: "no credentials, log in" versus "your `.glassfrogrc` is broken, fix it."
Treating a broken file as mere absence would send you down the wrong path, and
the project's Fail-Safe principle forbids letting a broken credential masquerade
as a missing one.

## Risk landscape

The resolution model was assessed for what could go wrong. Two risks were
accepted as residual (with mitigations); the rest were driven to low.

**The walk-up's intrinsic tradeoff.** Ascending to the filesystem root means a
`.glassfrogrc` planted in a shared or untrusted ancestor (a common workspace
root, a cloned repo, a `/tmp` subtree) would be discovered and its token used —
authenticating as an identity you didn't intend. This is the inherent cost of the
npm-style model the project deliberately chose. It can't be eliminated without
abandoning the model, so it's mitigated instead: the CLI reports which `Source`
and `Path` supplied the token (so a wrong-identity resolution is *visible*), and
`GLASSFROG_TOKEN` lets automation bypass file discovery entirely in untrusted
directories.

**Secret hygiene.** The token authenticates as a specific person, so leaking it
into a terminal, a CI transcript, or a log aggregator is a real compromise — and
error strings are exactly where a value being processed tends to leak. The
control is structural: errors and diagnostics carry only the file *path*, never
the token; only `Source` and `Path` are ever rendered. This is a contract carried
forward to Request Authentication, which handles the same secret on the request
side.

## Design boundaries

Several things Discovery deliberately does *not* do, and why:

- **It never writes a credentials file.** Writing is [Credential
  Storage](../reference/credential-storage.md)'s sole job. Two writers of one file
  would split the contract and let the read and write sides drift.
- **It never attaches the token or makes an API call.** That's Request
  Authentication's boundary; coupling transport into resolution would entangle two
  concerns.
- **It never decides an exit code or prompts interactively.** The consuming
  command owns exit-code classification; and because the operator is usually a
  non-interactive agent, a missing token is *reported*, never solicited — blocking
  on a prompt would hang automation.
- **It supports exactly one token — no profiles or per-host entries.** An API key
  is scoped to a single org + person, so a single resolved token is the whole
  need; multiplexing would add structure with no consumer.
